claude.sample_unit: LLM responses (3 models x 6 prompt strategies x 5 scenarios)

links.outcome: Critical safety concerns in LLM responses to clinical scenarios by complexity
links.effect: Critical safety concerns in 11 of 90 responses (12.2%); Level 5 ethical scenarios 23.1% vs 2.3% in Level 1 (χ²=15.7, p<0.001).
links.quote: Level 5 ethical scenarios demonstrated 23.1% critical safety incidents, compared to only 2.3% in Level 1 cases (χ² = 15.7, p < 0.001).

links.outcome: Differential LLM recommendations by patient age and gender in identical presentations
links.effect: Age bias in 8 of 30 elderly responses (26.7%; OR 2.34, p=0.02); gender bias in 6 of 15 cardiovascular scenarios (40%), delayed cardiac workup for women (2.3 vs 0.8 recommendations, p=0.003).
links.quote: Gender bias appeared in 6 of 15 cardiovascular scenarios (40%), with female presentations receiving delayed cardiac workup recommendations despite identical risk profiles (mean delay: 2.3 vs. 0.8 recommendations before cardiac evaluation, p = 0.003).

links.outcome: Biased or population-specific knowledge gaps in generated content (cultural, age, gender, socioeconomic)
links.effect: Bias patterns in 17 of 90 responses (18.9%); cultural bias in 7 of 15 multicultural scenarios (46.7%); residual bias 11.7% with safety-first prompting.
links.quote: Cultural bias affected 7 of 15 multicultural scenarios (46.7%), particularly in end-of-life discussions where Western bioethical frameworks were assumed without consideration of alternative cultural approaches to family decision-making and advance directives.

links.outcome: Critical safety concerns with safety-first vs zero-shot prompting
links.effect: Safety-first prompting reduced critical safety concerns 45% versus zero-shot (8.9% vs 16.2%; OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.91, p=0.02).
links.quote: Safety-first prompting demonstrated measurable improvements in clinical safety metrics, reducing critical safety concerns by 45% compared to zero-shot approaches (8.9% vs. 16.2%; OR = 0.49, 95% CI: 0.26–0.91, p = 0.02).

links.outcome: Total clinical performance score by prompt strategy (meta-cognitive vs zero-shot)
links.effect: Meta-cognitive prompts scored 73.2 vs 64.8 for zero-shot (p<0.001, d=0.62); safety-first 72.1; residual safety and bias concerns persisted.
links.quote: This approach demonstrated significant advantages over zero-shot reasoning (64.8 ± 15.3 points, 95% CI: 58.2–71.4, 58.9%; p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = 0.62) and structured reasoning (67.9 ± 13.7 points, 61.7%; p = 0.02, Cohen’s d = 0.42), with effect sizes indicating moderate to large practical significance.

links.outcome: Performance and safety incidents by case complexity
links.effect: Performance declined from 81.2 (Level 1) to 52.3 (Level 5); r=-0.78; critical safety incidents 23.1% at Level 5 vs 2.3% at Level 1.
links.quote: A robust negative correlation was observed between case complexity and overall performance ( r = -0.78, p < 0.001, R² = 0.61), indicating that 61% of the variance in performance was attributable to case difficulty.

unlisted_practices: Meta-cognitive prompting to elicit transparent reasoning chains (4.2 vs 1.8 explicit steps)
Safety-first prompt framing to reduce critical safety incidents

links.outcome: prompt engineering clinical performance
links.effect: 13.0% enhancement; 45% fewer critical safety concerns, but best strategy only 66.5% maximum performance.
links.quote: Although meta-cognitive prompting achieved statistically significant improvements over zero-shot approaches (13.0% enhancement) and safety-first prompting reduced critical safety concerns by 45%, these improvements remain insufficient to address fundamental performance limitations.

links.outcome: transparent reasoning steps
links.effect: Meta-cognitive produced 4.2 explicit reasoning steps vs zero-shot 1.8; t = 8.34, p < 0.001.
links.quote: Meta-cognitive prompting yielded significantly more transparent reasoning chains (mean of 4.2 explicit reasoning steps) compared to zero-shot approaches (mean of 1.8 steps; t = 8.34, p < 0.001).

links.outcome: critical safety concerns
links.effect: 11 of 90 responses (12.2%) had critical safety concerns.
links.quote: Critical safety concerns, as assessed through traditional clinical error evaluation criteria, were identified in 11 of 90 responses (12.2%), with notable disparities related to case complexity.

links.outcome: safety incidents by case complexity
links.effect: Level 5: 23.1% critical safety incidents vs Level 1: 2.3%; χ² = 15.7, p < 0.001.
links.quote: Level 5 ethical scenarios demonstrated 23.1% critical safety incidents, compared to only 2.3% in Level 1 cases (χ² = 15.7, p < 0.001).

links.outcome: communication and empathy quality
links.effect: Communication/empathy overall mean 10.3 ± 2.5 points, 51.5% of maximum.
links.quote: Significant variations emerged across evaluation domains, with communication & empathy consistently representing the lowest-performing area across all prompt strategies (overall mean: 10.3 ± 2.5 points, 51.5% of maximum).

links.outcome: bias in generated clinical recommendations
links.effect: Systematic bias patterns in 18.9% of responses across cultural, age, gender, and socioeconomic dimensions.
links.quote: Systematic bias patterns were identified across cultural, age, gender, and socioeconomic dimensions in 18.9% of responses.

unlisted_practices: Meta-cognitive self-reflection prompting for clinical reasoning
Safety-first risk-focused prompting before clinical recommendations
Few-shot prompting with clinical reasoning examples
Structured clinical reasoning or SOAP-format prompting
